title: Single-account login failure because account data missing from MongoDB Account collection (PL-48047)
diagnosis: A single account (knollinvestments) was unable to log in to Method because its account-level data had gone missing from the MongoDB Account collection. The data was restored by manually re-inserting it; PL-48047 was filed to investigate how the data was lost in the first place. Pattern is rare but recurring shape: when a single account can't sign in and everything else is healthy, check the Mongo Account collection for that account name.
playbook: 1) On 'single account cannot sign in / login' reports while the rest of the platform is healthy, query the MongoDB Account collection for that account's document. If it's missing, this is the pattern. 2) Mitigation: restore the missing document from a backup or recreate it manually if no backup exists. 3) Long-term: PL-48047 root-cause analysis — most likely candidates are a botched cleanup script or a TTL index misconfiguration.

title: Migration 672 (banner content/schedule collection creation across all accounts) overwhelmed Mongo + cascaded to App Update Agent → new accounts had blank dashboards (PL-58297)
diagnosis: Migration 672 ran synchronous drop/create operations on two collections (BannerContentCollection, BannerScheduleCollection) across all ~12K account databases at once, triggering WiredTiger's 'deferred table drop' mechanism and replication lag. The Mongo load cascaded to the App Update Agent (RabbitMQ consumer), which failed creating two compound indexes — AddCmpndIdxVersionIdToScreenInfoAccount (Runtime.Core.ScreenInfo) and AddCmpndIdxFieldTableNameToScreenBaseAccount (Runtime.Core.ScreenBase). New accounts finishing onboarding during the 2-hour window saw blank dashboards. Mitigation: P0 to stop the migration immediately; PL-58299 reshapes the migration to run off-hours; PL-58300 adds index-check handling.
playbook: 1) If new-account dashboards are blank during/after a migration window, check whether a migration script is currently running across all account DBs (look for active drop/create ops in Mongo). 2) Confirm App Update Agent failures via the RabbitMQ consumer logs and look for index-creation failures on Runtime.Core.ScreenInfo / Runtime.Core.ScreenBase. 3) Mitigation: stop the offending migration — apps re-appear instantly for new accounts once Mongo load subsides. 4) Long-term: any future cross-account migration must run off-hours and in smaller batches, and must NOT use synchronous drop+create (use create-only or rename-then-drop).

title: MongoDB rs01 self-aborts on file-descriptor exhaustion (LimitNOFILE=64000 too low)
diagnosis: LimitNOFILE=64000 in mongod.service (never overridden from the install default) is too low for the multi-tenant, one-DB-per-tenant deployment. Migration 716 (commit 23a3164) created two new collections in every tenant DB, pushing FD count past the limit. WiredTiger returned errno 24 (EMFILE), triggering fatal assertion 50882 and a self-abort. The replica set failed over in ~10 seconds, but rs01 stayed down for 91 minutes because Restart=on-failure was not set in the service unit, leaving all traffic on a single data node (causing slow customization screens). rs02 (current primary) was at ~27,300/64,000 FDs and rising at PIR time â€” same crash risk remains until LimitNOFILE is raised.
playbook: 1) Check mongod logs on rs01/rs02/rs03 for fatal assertion 50882 or 'errno 24' or 'EMFILE'. 2) Check current FD usage: `lsof -p $(pgrep mongod) | wc -l`. If approaching 64000, you're on the same path. 3) Check whether LimitNOFILE was raised: `systemctl show mongod | grep LimitNOFILE`. Per PIR action item (Arash, immediate priority), this should be raised to infinity and Restart=on-failure added via systemd drop-in (rs01 first, then step down rs02). 4) Symptom signal: 'customization slow' + only one healthy replica = rs01 (or whichever) is down. 5) Mitigation: manual restart of the failed mongod.

title: ms-account-api ClusterInfo / DbCluster lookup endpoint failing — downstream services can't resolve tenant DB clusters; usually caused by a TFS deploy regression

any_of.contains: Could not fetch ClusterInfo from account microservice

any_of.regex: Connect on AlocetSystem,[^:]+: Could not fetch ClusterInfo

diagnosis:
ms-account-api (Account.Api solution; per CLAUDE.md owns AlocetSystem cluster registry) serves the ClusterInfo lookup endpoint via V3ClusterController.GetAccountClusterInfoAsync at GET /v3/cluster/account?databaseName=<name>&client=<id>. Downstream services call this to determine which SQL cluster (C1-C5) a tenant DB lives on; without a successful ClusterInfo response they cannot open the tenant connection and cascade-fail every account-scoped operation. When ms-account-api returns 5xx or fails to respond in the timeout window, the failure shows up downstream as: (a) AuthService.GetProductFeatureFlag → TaskCanceledException (can't determine tenant for flag scope); (b) runtime-core → 'Could not determine DbClusterKey'; (c) SyncEngine → 'Could not fetch ClusterInfo from account microservice. dbName : <account>' with InvalidSyncResultException; (d) MSAuth/MSIdentity 502s from nginx (the call to ms-account-api at the microservices.method.int proxy fails to reach upstream). The proximate symptom is widespread microservices.method.int 502s and Newtonsoft 'Unexpected character <' deserialize errors — those are downstream of the ms-account-api deploy break.

Method deploys ms-account-api via Azure DevOps / TFS, NOT GitHub. The `gh api` will show NO recent commits even when a deploy regression caused the incident — because the deploy ran against an artifact built from an existing master commit on a separate schedule. Verify deploys via TFS Build IDs and the Method-Status-Deployment dashboard. On 2026-06-04 the most recent ms-account-api merges before the failed deploy were PR #1013 (PL-62910 IDOR fix re-release, June 2 — touches AccountStatusService) and PR #1014 (PL-62800 health check rework, May 29 — touches Startup.cs / Program.cs, high-risk startup wiring). PR #1014 is the more likely culprit per startup-wiring blast radius but requires TFS Build ID to confirm.
playbook:
**STEP 0 — Read the #swat thread FIRST.** Search the incident's swat thread for engineer messages naming a service for rollback (e.g., 'rolling back X', 'reverting X', 'X is the deploy that broke'). Engineer attribution beats every other signal for deploy-regression incidents because Method's TFS-based deploy pipeline is invisible to gh API. On 2026-06-04: Yuri's 'reverting ms-account' at 14:03 UTC → Nelson 'feels like we're back' at 14:08 UTC (5 min). If engineers have already named ms-account-api, your job is to verify and document, not re-derive.

1) Confirm the signature in ES: aggregate by Error.keyword over the alert window. Look for the co-occurrence of `Could not determine DbClusterKey` AND `Could not fetch ClusterInfo from account microservice` AND nginx-style 502s on `microservices.method.int`. All three together = ms-account-api ClusterInfo break.

2) Check ms-account-api's DD APM HIT-RATE, not just error-rate. `sum:trace.aspnet_core.request.hits{service:ms-account-api,env:prod}.as_count().rollup(sum,300)` over the alert window — a drop from baseline to near-zero for 3+ minutes is a P0 signal even when zero errors are logged (a service that crashed and stopped emitting traces shows zero hits AND zero errors). The DD monitors `Service ms-account-api has a high p90 latency on env:prod` and `... high average latency` will transition state at recovery time — use those modified timestamps to bracket the failure window.

3) Check IIS app pool state on MSL03 / MSL04 / MSL05 (the microservices nodes that host ms-account-api). `Get-IISAppPoolState <ms-account-pool>` from an admin shell. Look for: Stopped state, or recent w3wp.exe Application Event Log entries with Event ID 1000 (.NET unhandled exception during startup) or 1026 (.NET runtime crash).

4) Pull recent TFS Build IDs for ms-account-api from Azure DevOps. Identify which Build ran today, what git SHA it covered, and whether the deploy pipeline successfully passed /health/check verification post-deploy. PR #1014 introduced a /health/check that exposes Build/Release fields specifically for this kind of correlation — use it.

5) Mitigation: redeploy the previous known-good TFS artifact. Per 2026-06-04 this takes ~5 minutes to fully recover (faster than IIS pool recycles or DNS flushes). DO NOT attempt code-level fixes during the incident — get the bad bits off prod first.

6) Long-term (file as Jiras): A1) Wrap `HttpClient.SendAsync` to `*.method.int` hosts with Polly circuit breaker (5 consecutive 5xx, 30s open window). A2) Validate `Content-Type: application/json` before calling Newtonsoft.DeserializeObject — return typed `UpstreamRespondedWithHtml` error instead. A3) Add a per-account ClusterInfo cache with 5-min stale-while-revalidate in AuthService / runtime-core / SyncEngine. B1) Wire TFS deploys to post DD Events tagged `deploy: service:<svc> commit:<sha>` so deploy-correlation overlays work. B2) Add traffic-drop monitors (hits going from N/s to <10% of baseline for 3+min) on critical services. B4) Use the BuildMetadata that PR #1014 added to do canary deploys (one worker, verify SHA on /health/check, then roll the rest).
references: 2026-06-04 #swat thread: Michael Melo 14:11Z 'investigating'; Michael Melo 14:15Z 'rolling back preferences'; Michael Melo 14:26Z 'rolling back everything released today'; Michael Melo 14:31Z 'rolling back some projects can take ~45 mins'; Michael Melo 15:00Z 'rollback complete did not resolve' (after ms-preferences); Yuri Zirianov 15:03Z 'reverting ms-account'; Nelson De Miranda 15:08Z 'feels like we're back online?'; Michael Melo 15:10Z 'we should be back up'. Sequence proves ms-preferences rollback failed → ms-account revert succeeded.

Related bot KB entries: ki-microservices-method-int-upstream-502-bad-gateway (the broader 502 cascade pattern), ki-html-error-response-newtonsoft-deserialize-pattern (the Newtonsoft symptom on calling services), ki-dns-microservices-method-int-pps-quota (a DIFFERENT layer — DNS — explicitly NOT this incident).

Code references — ms-account-api: V3ClusterController.cs (the ClusterInfo endpoint), AutofacModule.cs (DI registration), Startup.cs (PR #1014 wiring changes), BuildMetadata.cs (PR #1014 added — usable for canary correlation).

title: ms-account-api release exhausts nginx 1024-connection soft limit during single-node rotation → login failures
diagnosis: During the morning release of ms-account-api, the deploy drained one instance at a time. While only one healthy instance remained behind the LB, the nginx process there hit its 1024 max-connections soft limit (other microservices on the same MSL host competed for the same nginx). Health checks failed, ms-account became unresponsive, dependents (Method-JWT issuance, sign-in) cascaded. Action items: raise the nginx soft limit on connections, add an extra node to the MSL pool, reduce method-ui's call rate to ms-account, schedule application-health review meetings with dev teams.
playbook: 1) On 'trouble logging into Method' or ms-account-api health check failures during a release rotation, check the nginx on the deploying MSL host — `ss -tn state established '( sport = :http )' | wc -l`. If it's near 1024, this is the pattern. 2) Mitigation: pause the rotation; bring an additional node into the LB; raise the nginx soft limit if not already done. 3) Long-term: confirm the nginx connections monitor / alert is in place.

title: ms-account-api on MSL-03 returns slow/200s during release because heartbeat-only health check passes before Redis is reachable
diagnosis: During an ms-account-api release on 2023-12-01, AWS target-group health checks hit /health/heartbeat and returned 200 immediately, so AWS put the new instance back into rotation. The service itself was still failing to query Redis (cache lookups timing out), so end-user requests landed on an effectively-unready instance and screens took ~30 seconds to load. Pattern: shallow heartbeat-only health check on a service whose hot path depends on Redis being warm.
playbook: 1) If ms-account-api shows slow loads right after a release, check whether the AWS target group is using /health/heartbeat (shallow) vs /health/check (deeper). Per PIR action item PL-44270, the AWS health-check path was updated to /health/check; verify it's still set that way. 2) If Redis is timing out, check Redis health and connectivity from the ms-account-api host first. 3) Long-term cache-timeout/retry improvements are tracked in PL-44341.

title: New-signup onboarding fails on first step when ms-preferences-api can't initialize preferences for unknown/renamed feature flag
diagnosis: Signup passes a list of feature flags to ms-preferences-api when creating an account. If any flag is unknown or has been renamed, ms-preferences-api fails the entire call — and ms-preferences has no mechanism to initialize the preferences collection on a partial failure. Result: new sign-ups error on the first onboarding page until ms-preferences-api is rolled back. Long-term fix: update preferences init to ignore unknown feature flags instead of failing.
playbook: 1) On 'new signups onboarding failing' reports, check whether ms-preferences-api was just released and whether the signup flow's feature-flag list includes any unknown/renamed flags. 2) Mitigation: roll back ms-preferences-api. 3) Long-term: confirm the preferences-init endpoint now ignores unknown feature flags (silently skip rather than fail the whole call).

title: Multi-tenant runtime pages with 'Call Routine' on load/focus fail to load after GetAppName cache change (PL-60985)
diagnosis: A change to improve cross-account app-name retrieval (GetAppName cache lookup) unintentionally exposed a pre-existing bug where some code paths used the wrong account reference when connecting to the per-tenant database. Tenants whose pages used 'Call Routine' actions on page load/focus (e.g., Invoice List, Sales Receipt List on mobilitycitybocaratonfl and JudicialServicesRR) failed to load. Mitigation: rolled the change back via PL-60985. Long-term: PL-60992 adds multi-tenant unit/automation tests for GetAppName and a fix for the underlying account-reference bug.
playbook: 1) If multi-tenant accounts report specific pages (often list pages with Call Routine actions on load) failing to load after a release, check whether the most recent runtime-core deploy touched the GetAppName cache logic in ServiceMap or related code paths. 2) Confirm by checking whether the affected accounts use Call Routine on page load/focus (mobilitycitybocaratonfl is a known reproducer with multiple tenant locations). 3) Mitigation: roll back the offending change. 4) Long-term: ensure PL-60992 unit/automation tests pass before merging similar cache-lookup changes.

title: CIAMedical SOAP API logging fails with 'Timeout expired … all pooled connections in use' from MySQL

match.tightening_note: 2026-06-10: required MySql in all_of (any pool/connection issue mentioning MySql), then CIAMedical-scoped OR explicit pool-exhaustion message OR 'Failed to log' + MySql together. Prevents firing on any unrelated MySQL exception without CIAMedical or logging context.

diagnosis: The CIAMedical SOAP API host exhausted its MySQL connection pool with 'Timeout expired. The timeout period elapsed prior to obtaining a connection from the pool. This may have occurred because all pooled connections were in use and max pool size was reached.' Other Classic hosts (4/5) had many users hitting MySQL with no effect. Impact was minimal — only the per-call count-logging failed (the API calls themselves still went through), so the only side effect was that customers got 'free' calls beyond their API limit. Mitigation: changed MySQL calls into a singleton, which silenced the noise.
playbook: 1) If logs on a SOAP API host (CIAMedical or similar) show 'MySql.Data.MySqlClient.MySqlException … all pooled connections were in use', check whether per-call logging is creating a new MySQL connection per request. 2) Confirm: API endpoint itself works, only count-logging fails. 3) Mitigation: make the MySQL connection a singleton (or use a connection-pool helper that reuses connections). 4) Customer impact is minimal — API limit tracking is broken (free calls until fixed).

title: oauth_token MongoDB at ~6 TB: daily MongoDB-Backup-Status-bot warning fire (5 GB advisory threshold)
diagnosis: Daily backup-completion notification from B05PN7JG87L (hypothesized MongoDB-Backup-Status bot per the 2026-05-31 investigation) flags the oauth_token Mongo DB as oversized whenever its on-disk size exceeds the 5 GB advisory threshold. Backup itself COMPLETES SUCCESSFULLY (white-check-mark in alert text); the warning is purely informational about future backup-window cost/throughput. Observed sizes: 6000.81 GB (2026-05-31T10:39:07Z) -> 6008.22 GB (2026-06-01T10:31:18Z) -> 6016.54 GB (2026-06-02T10:44:42Z) = +7.41 GB then +8.32 GB across the 3 sightings, avg ~7.8 GB/day, ~1203x the 5 GB threshold and rising linearly. Underlying root cause hypothesis (UNCONFIRMED): IdentityServer4 (oauth2 service) expired-access-token / refresh-token / persisted-grant cleanup job is not running, so the PersistedGrants / ReferenceTokens / DeviceFlowCodes collections accumulate indefinitely. The Method-JWT Redis cache is a separate concern -- this DB is the IdentityServer4 EF-Core operational store. Growth rate of ~7 GB/day extrapolates to ~2.5 TB/year of unbounded growth on top of the existing ~6 TB. The 5 GB threshold is a single global advisory tuned for typical Method tenant DBs (tens of MB to single-digit GB); oauth_token is the largest non-tenant Mongo DB in the fleet and will fire this monitor every day until either the cleanup runs or the advisory is excepted for this DB. No service outage and no customer-visible impact today; backup throughput cost is the only present concern.
playbook: 1) Verify alert is from bot_id B05PN7JG87L on #alert-system with text starting ':white_check_mark: *MongoDB Backup Completed with Warning*' -- this means BACKUP SUCCEEDED, the warning is informational. 2) Compare current GB to prior days' fires (incident-log.jsonl: alert_hash 280112c3596d9bcc on 2026-05-31 = 6000.81 GB; this entry tracks subsequent fires). If growth rate jumps materially (>20 GB/day), escalate -- otherwise treat as known steady-state. 3) Root-cause investigation (when capacity for it): SSH to the mongod cluster hosting oauth_token and run: mongo oauth_token --eval 'db.PersistedGrants.count(); db.ReferenceTokens.count(); db.DeviceFlowCodes.count()'; then check the Expiration field distribution to confirm whether expired grants are accumulating. 4) Fix options for owner team (oauth2 / ms-authentication-api): (a) enable IdentityServer4 TokenCleanupService (built-in, off by default in the EF-Core store); (b) add a scheduled Mongo TTL index on the Expiration field; (c) one-time deleteMany for already-expired grants to reclaim the bulk of the 6 TB. 5) Monitoring fix: either raise the 5 GB advisory threshold globally (loses small-DB signal), or add oauth_token to a per-DB exception list on the backup-status bot.

title: prod-new-04 intermittent 'Login is from an untrusted domain' SQL errors after gMSA 30-day password rotation

any_of.contains: Login is from an untrusted domain

diagnosis: Customers intermittently hit the Method error page; refreshing worked. Investigation showed the error originated on prod-new-04 (a recently added Windows server to help with release-time load): 'Login failed. The login is from an untrusted domain and cannot be used with Integrated authentication.' from method-platform-ui connecting to SQL. Root cause: the IIS app pools run under a group managed service account (prod_new_gmsa$). gMSA passwords rotate every 30 days by default, which coincided with the server's age. prod-new-04 had not been added to the AD group that grants access to the new gMSA password, so when the password rotated, the service account could not authenticate to SQL. Immediate fix: removed prod-new-04 from target group / LB. Permanent fix: added the server to the 'prod_new_gmsa' AD group and added Centreon health checks for the server's endpoints.
playbook: 1) If a specific node shows intermittent 'Login failed. The login is from an untrusted domain' SQL errors and it's a newer Windows server, check (a) whether the gMSA password rotated recently (default every 30 days) and (b) whether the host is a member of the AD group that grants password-retrieval permission. 2) Immediate mitigation: remove the failing node from the LB target group so traffic stops hitting it. 3) Permanent fix: add the host to the correct AD group, then Test-ADServiceAccount on the server to confirm gMSA retrieval works. 4) Centreon health checks should be added for every new prod node's endpoints; if missing, this kind of slow-rolling failure goes undetected for many hours.

title: QBDT Real-Time Sync silently fails because legacy-sync-services DNS routes to wrong machine in target group (PL-61643)

any_of.regex: connection attempt failed because the connected party did not properly respond

diagnosis: Customers reported Real-Time Sync from Method to QuickBooks Desktop was not working — QBDT instances showed as 'connected' but RT events were not triggering. Background, full, and changes syncs were unaffected. Root cause: DNS configuration for legacy-sync-services on prod-classic-1/2 resolved to a load balancer whose target group pointed to the WRONG machine, so RT-sync traffic was timing out or failing to reach the actual service. Temporary fix: added a host entry on prod-classic-1/2 to force traffic to the correct IP. Permanent fix: added the correct machine (prod-utility) to the target group, so DNS routing now works; the temporary host entries can be removed once the new routing is confirmed stable.
playbook: 1) If RT sync from Method→QBDT is down but background/full/changes sync still works, suspect a DNS routing problem (NOT an app-pool crash). 2) From prod-classic-1 and prod-classic-2, run `nslookup legacy-sync-services.method.int` and confirm the load balancer it resolves to has prod-utility in its target group. 3) Confirm via the canonical error: 'A connection attempt failed because the connected party did not properly respond after a period of time, or established connection failed because connected host has failed to respond'. 4) Mitigation: add an /etc/hosts (Linux) or hosts file (Windows) entry pointing legacy-sync-services to the correct prod-utility IP. 5) Permanent: AWS console → target group → add prod-utility, remove temp hosts entries.

title: QBO Sync silently fails to enqueue to RabbitMQ â€” Datadog trace + old MassTransit blockage
diagnosis: Real-time QBO sync goes silently dark: calls to the QBO Sync API are not landing in RabbitMQ for consumers to process. Recycling the app pool on Sync (Util 2 & 3) is required for messages to enqueue again. Root cause: combination of (a) MassTransit being out of date on the project and (b) Datadog's trace causing a blockage in coordination with MassTransit that prevents messages from going into Rabbit. Mitigation: Datadog's trace has been removed from QBO Sync. A code change by Arash exists to help prevent recurrence when Datadog trace is reattached. MassTransit upgrade is planned as part of the AI Upgrade work.
playbook: 1) If QBO real-time sync is reported as down, check RabbitMQ inbound queue depth for the QBO Sync exchange â€” if the publisher side is silent (no messages landing), this is the pattern. 2) Confirm by checking whether Datadog trace was recently re-enabled on QBO Sync (configuration / deploy history). 3) Mitigation: recycle app pools on Sync Util 2 & 3 (this clears the blockage temporarily). 4) Long-term: keep Datadog trace OFF on QBO Sync until MassTransit is upgraded (tracked under AI Upgrade).

title: RabbitMQ cluster memory leak — AuditTrail API health check holds persistent broker connection on every check (PL-57675)
diagnosis: The RabbitMQ cluster experienced prolonged high memory usage (4 days) traced to a connection leak in the AuditTrail API. Its health check was misconfigured to open a persistent connection to the broker on every probe; with frequent probes, the open-connection count grew continuously and consumed RMQ memory. Manual node restarts temporarily relieved memory pressure. The investigation was initially hampered because the old AWS Classic Load Balancer did not pass true client IPs. Resolution: replaced the CLB with an NLB to expose client IPs, identified MSL03/MSL04 as the offending services, fixed the AuditTrail health check, deployed. Long-term: PL-57581 migrates the RMQ cluster to new Ubuntu machines with the latest broker version. No customer impact during the incident — only internal alerting noise and manual restarts.
playbook: 1) On 'RabbitMQ memory growing / high memory' alerts, list the open RMQ connections by client IP. If a single host has dozens-to-hundreds of connections, that's the leak source. 2) If client IPs are masked by a CLB, fail back to the NLB-exposed view (or restart the LB to capture true IPs). 3) Identify the offending service (often AuditTrail API on MSL03/MSL04) and confirm via its health check route. 4) Mitigation: fix the health check to close its broker connection after probing (per PL-57675), redeploy. 5) Long-term: PL-57581 RMQ upgrade migration.

title: RabbitMQ goes critical when audit-trail queue fills from a large qbo-sync-api customer change burst
diagnosis: On 2023-11-27 a customer-driven qbo-sync-api pull of >50K accTaxCl* changes pushed massive audit-trail traffic through RabbitMQ. The audit-trail queue overflowed, processing fell behind, and the broker went Critical (linux-prod-01 hit high memory and failed; RabbitMQ nodes started reporting 'Node not responding / Removing (timedout) connection' in their logs). Services dependent on RabbitMQ went Critical and Method became briefly unresponsive. When the audit trail maxes out, audit entries can be lost.
playbook: 1) If RabbitMQ goes Critical and Method services are unresponsive, check RabbitMQ logs for 'Node ... not responding' / 'Removing (timedout) connection' patterns and check memory on linux-prod-01/02. 2) Aggregate audit-trail queue depth and identify the producing account (often qbo-sync-api pulling a big sync). 3) Mitigation: throttle / pause the offending customer sync; restart RabbitMQ nodes if they remain partitioned. 4) Long-term fix tracked in PL-44203.

title: Platform slowness from Redis SCAN spikes via CacheClearEventConsumer pattern-deletes
diagnosis: Sporadic platform slowness correlates with Redis CPU/latency spikes. Cause: CacheClearEventConsumer clears cache entries by pattern matching (e.g., 'UserContext:account:identity*', 'PreferenceContext:account:identity*'). On Redis/Valkey, pattern deletes require scanning the full keyspace to locate matching keys. Under high cache invalidation rates (coordinated user/permission changes), this generates burst SCAN commands across multiple shards, saturating Redis and degrading API response times for all customers. Duplicate cache-clear messages for the same account/identity are not coalesced â€” the same expensive scan executes many times in rapid succession.
playbook: 1) Confirm via Datadog Redis metrics: CPU spike + elevated SCAN command rate in the alert window. 2) Check for burst of CacheClearEventConsumer log entries. 3) Mitigation (short-term): no immediate fix â€” slowness resolves when the cache-clear burst subsides. 4) Long-term fix is tracked in PL-62474: (a) replace pattern-scan deletes with tag-based deletes maintaining Redis Set tags; (b) implement message coalescing so burst dupes collapse; (c) add Redis SCAN-rate alerting. Set CachingOptions.RunLegacyCacheClearPatternFallback=true during rollout, flush legacy untagged keys post-deploy, then disable the fallback.

title: IIS saturation during deploy rotation: 1.7k 401-burst to GetUtcOffsetFromTimezone overflows app-pool queue while single-node
diagnosis: During the 8:55 AM scheduled release rotation, a frontend bug triggered a burst of ~1.7k requests to the GetUtcOffsetFromTimezone endpoint. Those requests returned 401 Unauthorized; method-ui was configured to throw .NET exceptions for 401s, and .NET exceptions are computationally expensive. Because the deploy was mid-rotation, only one node was in the LB. That single node's IIS saturated almost instantly, the app-pool queue overflowed, and the platform showed white screens / freezes for ~45 min. User refreshes amplified the load. Action items per PIR: extend deploy/deregister delay by +60s, change method-ui to return response codes instead of throwing exceptions for 401, add WAF rate-limit rules based on Athena log analysis, optimize GetUtcOffsetFromTimezone, consider keeping a spare node during the deploy rotation.
playbook: 1) On 'white screen' / IIS-saturation alerts during a release window, check whether the LB shows only one healthy node (mid-rotation single-node state). 2) Search ES for a burst of 401s in the window — especially for GetUtcOffsetFromTimezone or any endpoint that returns 401 for unauthenticated calls. 3) If both signals hit, the pattern is confirmed. 4) Mitigation: bring an additional node into the target group, or pause the rotation, until the burst subsides. 5) Long-term: confirm WAF rate-limits are enforced and method-ui no longer throws .NET exceptions for non-2xx HTTP status (action item from this PIR).

title: Report Designer 404 for specific users/accounts after method-ui hotfix (transient config corruption on release) (PL-46633)
diagnosis: A method-ui hotfix release caused intermittent 404s in the Report Designer for specific users/accounts. The code change itself was unrelated to the report designer. Not reproducible on dev environments. Re-releasing the same code resulted in no issues. Final hypothesis: a release-pipeline glitch caused config-file corruption / inconsistent copy during the deploy. Action item: DevOps to investigate the release pipeline.
playbook: 1) On 'Report Designer 404 for some accounts/users' alerts right after a method-ui release, check whether the deployed config files match the expected SHA across all method-ui hosts. If any host has a corrupted or inconsistent config file, this is the pattern. 2) Mitigation: re-release the same code (the PIR confirms re-release works). 3) Long-term: DevOps investigation into release-pipeline reliability (no ticket linked at PIR time).

title: REST API developer docs blank page — CDN removed redoc.standalone.js (PL-58656)

match.tightening_note: 2026-06-10: removed bare 'RestAPI' / 'Rest API developer documents' matches and the loose 'REST.API.*blank' regex. Required either explicit redoc.standalone.js / PL-58656 evidence OR a REST API + missing-asset signal in conjunction. Prevents firing on any unrelated REST API outage.

diagnosis: The CDN hosting redoc.standalone.js (used by Method's REST API developer-docs page to render the API spec) removed the file at the location we were referencing, so the docs page rendered as a blank white page. REST API itself was unaffected — only the developer-docs UI was down. Discovered internally before any customer reported it; hotfixed by repointing the script tag to redoc's new CDN location.
playbook: 1) On 'REST API docs blank page' reports, view-source the docs page and check for the redoc.standalone.js <script> tag — if the URL returns 404, the CDN has moved the file. 2) Hotfix: update the script tag to redoc's current CDN URL (or self-host redoc.standalone.js in Method's static assets to remove the third-party CDN dependency). 3) The REST API endpoints themselves are unaffected — communicate that to customers if asked.

title: runtime-core morning deploy stalls on Ansible failure; retry overwhelms restarted services with Redis-timeout burst
diagnosis: During the morning runtime-core API deploy on 2025-05-20, the Ansible deploy machine failed, the retry took a long time, and code versions diverged across the four runtime machines. When the runtime-core services finally restarted simultaneously, the burst of waiting requests overwhelmed the freshly-cold pool. A high volume of Redis timeouts compounded the slowness. Two parallel mitigations were started: migrating Ansible to its own server (so a single Ansible failure doesn't stall the deploy) and creating a new Redis cluster for tables-and-fields and the heaviest Redis users.
playbook: 1) On 'runtime-core outage' alerts during a morning release window, check whether Ansible is the deploy runner and whether it just failed/retried. 2) Confirm via version skew across the four runtime machines (check deployed git SHA on each). 3) Confirm Redis timeout volume in DD (search for Redis.*timeout in runtime-core logs). 4) Mitigation: wait for the deploy to converge, then warm caches; in severe cases reduce LB capacity to a subset of nodes until cache warms. 5) Long-term: confirm Ansible is on a dedicated host (not shared with anything else) and that the new Redis cluster has been carved out for tables-fields / heavy users.

title: runtime-core-api 404s on one node after re-registration because AWS target group default port is 5000 instead of 80
diagnosis: On 2025-05-14 a memory alert on prod-rt-04 (driven by AppRoutine.Subscriber.Agent slowly leaking) led DevOps to remove the host from the production-runtime-core-api target group, restart it, and re-register it. The target group's default protocol port was 5000, so the re-added host registered on 5000 instead of 80. Requests that landed on rt4 then 404'd, producing intermittent blank screens / slowness for all users. Two parallel fixes: (1) PL-54148 fixes the AppRoutine memory leak; (2) PL-54150 moved runtime-core-api to a new target group with the correct default port.
playbook: 1) If runtime screens are intermittently blank/404 after a runtime-core node was just restarted or re-registered, suspect a port-mismatch on the AWS target group. 2) Verify each registered runtime-core-api target is on port 80 (not 5000). 3) Mitigation: re-register the host with the correct port. 4) Long-term: per PIR, runtime-core-api now lives in a target group whose default port is correct; verify that's still the case in AWS console.

title: runtime-core repeatedly calls ms-account endpoint after PL-57225 broke ServiceMap cache → platform slowness (PL-57626 hotfix)
diagnosis: A runtime-core change in PL-57225 (app-publish / app-update logic) modified ServiceMap class caching behavior such that runtime-core skipped its in-memory cache for the ms-account lookup and queried ms-account on every request. Excess runtime→ms-account traffic increased load on backend systems and caused platform-wide slowness for ~4h35m, particularly during app publish/update operations. Hotfix PL-57626 restored proper caching.
playbook: 1) On platform slowness alerts after a runtime-core release, check the request rate from runtime-core to ms-account in Datadog. If it's 10-100x baseline, ServiceMap caching is broken. 2) Verify the most recent runtime-core deploy touched ServiceMap or related cache code (check PL-57225 / PL-57626 history). 3) Mitigation: deploy a hotfix that restores the original ServiceMap caching, or roll back the offending PR. 4) Verify in Warehouse and prod that the request rate returned to baseline.

title: SendGrid sub-user suspension after malicious Method tenant sends phishing/spam through it (recurring: Feb 11 / Apr 14 / Apr 21 2026)
diagnosis: SendGrid Fraud Ops repeatedly suspends Method's outbound sub-users (Sub-User 2 / OpsSubUser) after detecting phishing from a Method tenant. The pattern: a malicious or compromised customer account sends phishing through Method's shared SendGrid identity, SendGrid suspends the entire sub-user, all Method customers without an authenticated custom domain stop delivering email until traffic is rerouted to a different sub-user. Confirmed occurrences in 2026: Feb 11 (Sub-User 2, statewidehireptyltd, ~6 days outage until reactivation), Apr 14 (OpsSubUser, ranksizexxl.club from tenant wanddgital), Apr 21 (OpsSubUser, tanamcmullan.com phishing from fmpublicationsltd via leftover attacker user METHODE from a prior Tunisia incident). Root cause is structural: no outbound email content inspection, no tenant rate limiting for new sign-ups, no anomaly detection for attacker-style changes (new users, API keys, owner-email change to non-matching domain). Reactivation requires API-key deletion, password rotation, and 2FA per SendGrid's non-negotiable steps; Basic support plan slows response.
playbook: 1) If transactional/marketing emails are stuck in 'Pending' or being deferred, check SendGrid dashboard for sub-user suspension state. 2) Identify the offending Method account from SendGrid's suspension reason (it always names a tenant domain). Disable that tenant's MethodId+users, rotate API keys, invalidate owner sessions, audit for leftover attacker users (the Apr 21 case had a stale 'METHODE' user from a prior compromise). 3) Immediate mitigation: reroute outbound from the suspended sub-user to a healthy one (SubUser2 / SubUser3) and confirm queue drains. 4) Submit remediation evidence to SendGrid (API-key rotation, password reset, 2FA) and request reinstatement. 5) Long-term tracked in PL-61115: outbound payload inspection, new-signup tenant rate limiting, stricter domain validation, dynamic sub-user/IP management.

title: Authenticated-domain emails route to wrong sub-user because an old SendGrid sub-user agent was reactivated by server patching (PL-45779)
diagnosis: Some emails from customers with authenticated domains were not being properly authenticated and were going through the wrong SendGrid sub-user. Investigation found that during a server-patching restart, an old SendGrid sub-user subscriber agent on linux-prod-1 and linux-prod-2 (that had been disabled and removed from the service catalog) came back to life. So instead of 4 valid agents, 5 total were running — 1 of which was the invalid old one — and ~20% of outbound was being directed to that wrong sub-user. Fix: removed the code and disabled the service.
playbook: 1) On 'authenticated-domain emails landing in spam / wrong sender' reports, check the live SendGrid subscriber agents on linux-prod-1/2. If there are more than 4, an old agent has been reactivated. 2) Mitigation: disable / remove the extra agent. 3) Long-term: confirm the agent's code and service have been fully removed (not just disabled) so a patching restart can't bring it back.

title: Shuttle (third-party payment platform) outages disrupt Method payment widget / webhooks / portal — recurring
diagnosis: Method's payment integration depends on the third-party Shuttle platform. Shuttle has produced multiple recurring outages with the same Method-side signal — payment widget returns 504 / black screen / 500, webhooks stop, sometimes the Shuttle dev portal can't log in. Confirmed events: 2023-11-15 (PL-44065, bad Shuttle release E008 null), 2024-01-19 (~12h, Shuttle datacenter routing failure), 2024-02-14 (PL-45556, BOLT-1178, England Logistics specific config issue from Shuttle), 2024-10-08 (PL-49765, 24h full Shuttle outage from DB restore failure), 2024-10-29 (~48h Authorize.Net gateway behind Shuttle failing OAuth refresh during 7-day maintenance window). Pattern is third-party — Method has no remediation beyond communicating to customers and verifying the issue resolves on Shuttle's side. Action item history: investigate moving away from Shuttle and improving long-window alerting for third-party silent outages.
playbook: 1) On 'payments failing' / 'BOLT-1178' / 'Payment widget 504' reports, first check Shuttle's status page — if they have an open incident, this is the third-party pattern. 2) Confirm the Method-side signal: 504 gateway / 500 internal server error on the payment widget; webhook delivery dropping. 3) Mitigation: there's no Method-side fix during a Shuttle outage. Communicate the workaround to customers (wait for Shuttle to recover; processing resumes automatically). 4) Track recurrence — if Shuttle outages persist, escalate the 'move away from Shuttle' workstream.

title: Brief sign-in 400 errors during a sign-in hotfix release (HMAC validation transient failure) (PL-53896)
diagnosis: Admin team released a hotfix for the sign-in path. During the 2-minute deploy window, ~29 users got 400 errors on sign-in; the error logs pointed to HMAC validation failing. Users were able to sign in successfully shortly after. Action item: implement a sign-in fail-safe so HMAC checks can survive mid-release state without 400-ing customers.
playbook: 1) On a brief burst of sign-in 400s during/right after a release window, check whether the release touched the sign-in path. 2) Search for 'HMAC' in the sign-in logs in the window — if HMAC validation is throwing, this is the pattern. 3) No immediate action needed in most cases (transient; resolves within minutes). 4) Long-term: confirm the fail-safe action item is in place so this doesn't recur on the next sign-in hotfix.

title: Pausing/resuming one customer's stock app routine pauses it globally because JobSchedule filter omitted AccountId
diagnosis: Stock app routines (work orders, proposals, donations, etc.) are stored globally in MethodAppStore and referenced by individual accounts, but the JobSchedule documents are per-account. The pause/resume implementation filtered on AppRoutineId only, not on (AppRoutineId, AccountId), so a pause/resume in any single account (including dev/test accounts) flipped the schedule entries for every account referencing that global routine. The bug went unnoticed until a significant drop in routine executions was observed post-2025-06-10.
playbook: 1) If multiple customers across accounts report a stock app routine 'silently stopped', check JobSchedule pause/resume history and look for an action that hit AppRoutineId without an AccountId filter. 2) Mitigation: re-enable affected stock app routines via the templatedevv2 interface (per PIR). 3) Long-term fix already merged (PL-55177): the filter now uses AccountId together with AppRoutineId so per-account toggles stay scoped to that account.

title: MSN01/MSN02 crash from stock-app release surge + ms-search CPU contention on tables-fields microservice
diagnosis: Multiple StockApp releases on 2025-01-02 surged tables-fields-microservice request rate. ms-search-api separately was intermittently consuming excess CPU. The two services co-located on MSN01 and MSN02 competed for CPU, both servers crashed and restarted. Mitigation: ms-search refactor + upgrade to .NET 8 to fix performance bottlenecks, temporary MSN box upsize, and reverted recent ms-search changes.
playbook: 1) On MSN01/MSN02 crash alerts with no obvious deploy correlation, check whether multiple StockApp releases ran the same day and whether ms-search-api is showing high CPU. 2) Confirm via Datadog CPU graphs for tables-fields-api and ms-search on MSN01/02. 3) Mitigation: temporary box upsize, recycle app pools, throttle StockApp release cadence. 4) Long-term: keep ms-search on .NET 8 and consider splitting ms-search and tables-fields-microservice onto separate hosts.

title: Invalid ReceivePayment accounting logs created when customer cancels from within the Shuttle payment widget — stock-app execution change didn't handle widget cancellations (PL-54549)
diagnosis: A change to the stock-app execution logic did not properly account for payment cancellations initiated from within the Shuttle payment widget, so the system erroneously created ReceivePayment accounting logs when a customer cancelled mid-widget. ReceivePayment is a highly sensitive accounting field. Impact: ~38 accounts likely affected, 86 total erroneous payment logs created (plus some additional ones manually corrected by customers). The defect went undetected because there was no automation and no logging that would catch erroneous accounting writes of this kind — it was customer-reported, not alert-driven. Per the PIR, root cause was process-level rather than infrastructural: (1) missing requirements and test cases, (2) team rushing to hit deadlines, and (3) limited team knowledge of stock-app edge cases. Tracked as PL-54549.
playbook: 1) On customer reports of incorrect/duplicate ReceivePayment (payment) accounting logs shortly after a stock-app or Shuttle-widget change, suspect a cancellation path the stock-app execution change didn't handle (specifically cancelling from within the widget). 2) Scope the blast radius — identify affected accounts and the erroneous logs (last incident: ~38 accounts / 86 logs) and coordinate manual correction of the accounting records with affected customers. 3) This is a code/process defect, not infra: confirm the offending stock-app change and add the missing cancellation test case before re-release. 4) Longer-term per PIR: invest in unified hybrid-app dev practices (training, collaboration, knowledge-sharing on stock apps) and add monitoring plus more detailed post-sprint checks so erroneous accounting writes are caught automatically (none existed at incident time).

title: Entity updates wrote TenantId=null because PL-58920 column-restriction excluded system columns (PL-59906 hotfix)
diagnosis: The PL-58920 fix for an IndexOutOfRangeException added explicit column selection on entity retrieval queries: .Select(columnNames) where columnNames came from PrimaryTableFields (entity metadata). TenantId is a system-level DB column not exposed in entity metadata, so it was excluded from the query results — entity was read with TenantId=null, and subsequent updates persisted that null back. Data impact: ~30 records across 3 accounts (out of ~8.2M update operations in the Dec 22-29 window). PL-59906 was a hotfix removing the explicit column selection. PL-59920 backfills/repairs the corrupted records.
playbook: 1) If reports/audit-trail show TenantId=null on recently-updated entity records, check whether PL-58920-style column-restriction logic was deployed recently. 2) Confirm via DB: query the relevant entity table for TenantId IS NULL on rows updated in the window. 3) Hotfix: remove explicit column selection in entity retrieval — system columns (TenantId, etc.) MUST be in the result set. 4) Cleanup: run the PL-59920-style migration to restore TenantId from AuditTrail records. 5) Long-term: any entity-retrieval code that restricts columns must explicitly include system columns.

title: Intermittent failures on App-Builder / Grid Builder v2 because TFS release definition wasn't updated when a new AWS target-group node was added
diagnosis: A new node had been added to the AWS target group for App-Builder, but the TFS release definition was not updated to include the new machine, so the new node never received the latest application code. Customers saw intermittent failures in Grid Builder v2 (load balancer routed some requests to the stale node). Mitigation: updated the primary TFS release definition to include the new machine; also updated all future-ready release definitions; verified successful deploy across all nodes.
playbook: 1) On intermittent failures in any TFS-built service (App-Builder, etc.) immediately after target-group changes, list the target-group members in AWS and cross-check against the TFS release definition's deployment targets. 2) Confirm by sampling a request and identifying which node served it — if mismatched nodes return different behavior, this is the pattern. 3) Mitigation: redeploy via the corrected TFS release definition (or temporarily remove the stale node from the target group). 4) Long-term: any time a node is added to an AWS target group, DevOps must update every TFS release definition that targets that group.

title: Windows .NET Framework patching without reboot silently breaks app pools on MSN02 days later (PL-44252)
diagnosis: During the morning tables-fields release on 2023-11-29, the deploy failed health check on MSN02 (MSN01 was healthy). swat reports started coming in about the screen designer being unresponsive. Recycling the app pool unblocked the rollback. Investigation found that ms-archive-api on MSN02 had also been silently failing since 2023-11-23 (no logs/activity), while its heartbeat/health check stayed green. Root cause: Aqueel patched .NET Framework on MSN02 on the night of 2023-11-22 without rebooting the server. The patch required app pools to be recycled (or the server rebooted) before some services would resume functioning correctly. Action: monthly patching paused; long-term, patching steps must include auto-recycle/restart of app pools and ideally a server reboot.
playbook: 1) On 'tables-fields / screen designer unresponsive' or new release failing health check on one MSN host but not another, check whether Windows .NET Framework patching was recently applied without a reboot. 2) Confirm via Application Event Logs on the failing MSN — look for errors on the date matching the patch (e.g., Aqueel's Nov 22 patch). 3) Mitigation: recycle the affected app pool (Aqueel's Nov 29 step), then re-deploy. 4) Long-term: confirm the patching procedure now includes app-pool recycle + server reboot.

title: Yahoo automated systems block Method's outbound SendGrid IPs after high-volume campaign send (PL-47997 / PL-45894 / PL-47999)
diagnosis: Yahoo/AOL automated systems intermittently block Method's outbound SendGrid IPs when one IP sends 'too much mail' or 'too much bad quality mail' (e.g., spam complaints). Pattern: a single customer (often newly authenticated domain user) sends a large campaign (~10-20k recipients), the IP gets flagged, deliverability drops for all customers behind that IP. Mitigations: disable the flagged IP, divert traffic to backup IPs — but the diversion can propagate the block to the backup IP (PL-47997→PL-47999). Confirmed events: PL-45894 (Mar 19 2024, majesticturbodallas, ~12h), PL-47997 (Jul 25 2024, IP 167.89.91.86, ~14h), PL-47999 (Jul 26 2024, IP 149.72.215.137 after diversion, 30min). Long-term work: IP warm-up monitoring, bulk-email-limit/queue-fairness policy.
playbook: 1) On 'Yahoo/AOL deliverability drop' or 'emails to Yahoo failing' reports, check the SendGrid suppression / block list and the Yahoo postmaster page for the affected IPs. 2) Identify which customer drove the volume (usually a single newly-authenticated domain sending tens of thousands of recipients). 3) Mitigation: disable the flagged IP, divert traffic to a different IP — but monitor that traffic doesn't propagate the block to the new IP. 4) Long-term: enforce bulk-email-limit + queue-fairness policy; alert on per-IP send volume.
